reason: The core of the story—the heat probe's failure to dig deep enough after two years of attempts—is only supported by one site ([S1]). Sources [S5] and [S6] are pre-launch articles describing the probe's intent, while [S2] and [S4] focus on seismic results and do not mention the probe's unsuccessful outcome.
story: NASA’s InSight lander traveled to Mars to take the planet’s 'pulse' and 'temperature.' To do it, it carried a self-hammering probe nicknamed 'the mole,' designed to burrow 16 feet deep. But the $830 million mission was nearly derailed before it even left Earth. A vacuum leak just nanometers wide—so small it would take 50 years to deflate a car tire—forced a two-year delay and added $150 million to the bill. In 2018, InSight finally became the first interplanetary mission to launch from the US West Coast. While the lander successfully recorded the first-ever sounds of Martian wind and detected hundreds of marsquakes, 'the mole' struggled for two years. It was designed for soft soil but encountered terrain that lacked the friction needed to dig. After burying itself just a few centimeters, the team finally gave up, leaving the probe’s primary goal a dream buried in the Martian dust.
angle: A vacuum leak the size of an atom cost NASA $150 million and nearly killed the mission to hear the 'pulse' of Mars.

claims.claim: InSight stands for Interior Exploration using Seismic Investigations, Geodesy and Heat Transport.
The InSight mission launched on May 5, 2018.
InSight successfully landed on Mars on November 26, 2018.
The landing site was located at Elysium Planitia.
InSight was the first American interplanetary mission to launch from the United States West Coast.
A nanometer-sized vacuum leak in the SEIS instrument caused the mission to be delayed from 2016 to 2018.
The launch delay added an estimated $150 million to the mission's total cost.
The total mission cost was between $800 million and $830 million.
The mission included two briefcase-sized CubeSats named MarCO that were the first of their kind in deep space.
InSight used a 1.8-meter robotic arm to place its scientific instruments on the surface.
The Heat Flow and Physical Properties Package (HP3) probe was nicknamed 'the mole.'
The mole was designed to burrow 5 meters, or 16 feet, below the Martian surface.
The probe used a self-hammering mechanism to dig into the crust.
The HP3 instrument was provided by the German Aerospace Center (DLR).
InSight recorded the first sounds of Martian wind ever heard.
The mission officially ended in December 2022.
The lander lost power because Martian dust accumulated on its solar panels.
Seismic data from InSight confirmed that Mars has a molten core.
The lander detected a seismic event (S0976a) originating from active faults in Valles Marineris.

disputed: The total mission cost is cited as $830 million by S1 and approximately $800 million by S5; the script should attribute this as 'over $800 million.'

The weight of the MarCO CubeSats is stated as 13.5 kg in S1, while S7 gives a lower estimate for general 6U CubeSats; the script should use the specific MarCO weight from S1 or stick to 'briefcase-sized.'
The analogy that the leak would take 50 years to deflate a tire is only found in S6 and should be attributed as 'one expert estimate.'
